demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Mateo Rivera had always trusted his hands to read the wind and the timber. Three years ago, while guiding a heavy steel cable over a ridge in the northern woods, his grip slipped. The cable snapped back, striking his foreman, Marcus, in the shoulder with enough force to shatter the joint. Standing there with the cordite smell of the equipment yard hanging in the air, Mateo felt a cold certainty settle in his chest. There was something inherently faulty about him, a quiet defect in his focus that had translated directly into broken bone. He had come to believe that his hands, once reliable, had betrayed him. Even in the days immediately following, while Marcus recovered in the county hospital, Mateo found himself unable to relax in his own kitchen, his muscles held tight as if bracing for another falling load. The injury became a compass point for Mateo’s days. He walked into the forester’s supply depot and felt physical pain flare along his own left shoulder whenever a younger crew member reached overhead to grab a harness. The ache was not an injury of his own, but a somatic echo of what had happened to Marcus. He began avoiding the upper shelves, stepping back rather than risking another tangle. When he saw Marcus’s limp, or heard the particular clack of his prosthetic brace, memories of the victim surfaced with startling clarity. Mateo was certain that proximity mattered. At the monthly crew breakfasts, he would retreat to the edges of the room, watching the others approach the table, his body tensing as he calculated the space between them. He was not alone, but he could not relax in the crowd. Outside the woods, the world felt increasingly porous. Strangers pushing past him in the grocery aisle triggered a low, steady warning; he watched them closely for any sign that they might stumble into him or demand something he could no longer give. His own body mirrored the old moment. When the memory of the snapping cable rose, he felt his shoulders hunch and his knees lock, occupying the exact posture he had held when the weight swung toward Marcus. In those quiet hours, two currents would surge through him. First, a sharp rage at the suddenness of the accident, at the way his momentary lapse had unraveled so much. Then, quickly following, a heavy grief that left him sitting in his truck long after the engine cooled. He was certain that he could not rely on himself to catch what was coming, and the knowledge settled over him like a wet wool coat. His work as a forester, once the architecture of his days, gradually narrowed. He still came to the county offices and walked the timber plots, but he stopped taking the lead on heavy lifts. He delegated the cable checks to younger men, watching them from a careful distance rather than stepping into the swing zone. What frightened him most was the accumulation of these small retreats. His wife, Clara, noticed how he paused before opening heavy doors, how he flinched when she reached for his hand without warning. The equipment yard, where he had once moved with effortless authority, became a place of calculation. He would stand by the loading dock, feeling the phantom pull of the cable, his breath shallow, certain that one misstep would prove his incapacity to the rest of the crew. He was no longer capable of the work that had defined him for twenty years, not because the woods had changed, but because his own expectations of his body had shifted. Now, at fifty-four, Mateo sits in the waiting room of the community clinic, a referral from his primary care physician who noted the persistent somatic complaints and the unexplained fatigue. He holds his wife’s hand, but his gaze tracks the door, measuring who might enter next. He has come to seek help not because the pain is unbearable, but because the waiting has grown too heavy. He does not know if the dread he feels when a new hire approaches his desk is a warning or simply the echo of a broken cable, but he is tired of bracing. What he hopes for is a way to stand in a room without feeling the weight settle on his shoulders, to trust that his hands and his judgment can meet the day without failing him again.
